docs.title: ragpick
docs.text:
Choose, build, evaluate, and run the right RAG architecture.

Most RAG projects don't fail because of the LLM. They fail because the architecture was picked by guesswork: vector search where exact product codes matter, no access control for internal documents, no evidence that the "improved" pipeline is actually better.

ragpick turns that choice into an engineering process:

  1. Describe your requirements (corpus size, keyword-heavy queries, latency, access control) and ragpick recommend explains which blueprint fits and why.
  2. Define the pipeline as YAML. Architecture as code, validated with readable errors.
  3. Evaluate competing blueprints on your data with ragpick eval and pick the winner from numbers, not vibes.

ragpick sits next to LangChain and LlamaIndex rather than replacing them. It owns the interfaces, config, selector and evaluation; other libraries plug in as components.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install ragpick              # core, offline components
pip install "ragpick[openai]"    # + OpenAI embeddings and chat models
pip install "ragpick[all]"       # + sentence-transformers, Qdrant, PDF

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Concepts: components, blueprints, the selector, access control.
  • Blueprints: what each architecture is good at.
  • Config reference: every rag.yaml key.
  • Writing a plugin: add your own loader, store, or model.
  • Evaluation: metrics and how to compare configs.
  • Design decisions: the choices behind v0.1.

docs.title: LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters
docs.text:
ragpick works alongside LangChain and LlamaIndex rather than replacing them. Any of their loaders, embedding models, retrievers and LLMs can be used as a ragpick component, with ragpick's config, access control, selector and evaluation around it.

Neither framework is a ragpick dependency. The adapters only call public methods (embed_documents, invoke, get_text_embedding_batch, retrieve, …), so install the LangChain or LlamaIndex packages you want yourself:

pip install ragpick langchain-openai          # or: pip install ragpick llama-index
Kind type: langchain wraps type: llamaindex wraps loader a document loader (lazy_load() / load()) a reader (load_data()), default SimpleDirectoryReader embedder Embeddings (embed_documents, embed_query) an embedding model (get_text_embedding_batch, get_query_embedding) retriever a retriever (invoke(query)) a retriever (retrieve(query)) generator a chat model (invoke(messages)) an LLM (complete(prompt))

docs.title: From YAML
docs.text:
Give the class's import path and its constructor arguments:

blueprint: hybrid
components:
  loader:
    type: langchain
    params:
      class_path: langchain_community.document_loaders.PyPDFLoader
      path_arg: file_path               # the constructor argument that receives the path
  embedder:
    type: langchain
    params:
      class_path: langchain_openai.OpenAIEmbeddings
      kwargs: {model: text-embedding-3-small}
  generator:
    type: llamaindex
    params:
      class_path: llama_index.llms.openai.OpenAI
      kwargs: {model: gpt-4o-mini, temperature: 0}

class_path accepts package.module.Class or package.module:Class. A missing package fails with a clear "could not import … install the package" message.

Treat configs as code

class_path imports and instantiates arbitrary Python classes. Only load rag.yaml files you trust, just as you would only run code you trust.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
Pass objects you've already built:

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI, OpenAIEmbeddings
from ragpick import Pipeline, load_config
from ragpick.adapters import LangChainEmbedder, LangChainGenerator

pipeline = Pipeline(
    load_config("rag.yaml"),
    components={
        "embedder": LangChainEmbedder(embeddings=OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small")),
        "generator": LangChainGenerator(chat_model=ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")),
    },
)

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Generators use ragpick's grounded prompt and citation parsing, and also work as an evaluation judge (eval.judge: {type: langchain, params: {...}}). LangChain token usage comes from usage_metadata; LlamaIndex usage is estimated.
  • Embedders use the framework's query-embedding method for searches and its document-embedding method for indexing.
  • Loaders turn source / file_path metadata into document ids relative to the ingested path. When one file yields several documents (PDF pages), :<n> is appended.
  • Retrievers are for indexes managed outside ragpick. External retrievers can't apply ragpick filters, so filters and allowed_groups access control are applied to their results afterwards (post-filtering). Configure the external retriever to return enough candidates for that. Missing scores become 1 / rank.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
Run ragpick blueprints to see this list in your terminal.

Blueprint Status Best for naive stable prototypes, small corpora, natural-language questions over prose hybrid stable the default for commercial systems; keyword-heavy domains; medium and large corpora parent_child stable long structured documents where answers need surrounding context sql stable structured data and analytics questions (text-to-SQL) graph stable multi-hop and "main themes" questions (GraphRAG local + global search) agentic stable multi-part and comparison questions needing several lookups multimodal planned images, charts and scanned pages inside documents corrective stable noisy corpora, high-stakes answers: grade retrieval, retry, or refuse

docs.title: naive
docs.text:
directory loader → recursive chunker (800/100) → embedder → memory store
→ vector retriever → generator

The simplest architecture that works. Its weak spot is exact terms: an embedding of "E-4017" is barely different from "E-4071", so error codes, SKUs and legal references are often missed.

docs.title: hybrid
docs.text:
┌→ vector search ─┐
query (+ ACL filters) ─┤                 ├→ RRF fusion → [cross-encoder] → generator
                       └→ BM25 search ───┘

BM25 catches exact terms and vectors catch paraphrases. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines the two rankings without score calibration:

score(chunk) = Σ_lists  weight / (rrf_k + rank)        (rrf_k = 60 by default)

Tune it in your config:

blueprint: hybrid
components:
  retriever:
    params: {k: 20, rrf_k: 60, candidates: 40, vector_weight: 1.0, keyword_weight: 1.0}
  reranker: {type: cross_encoder}          # pip install "ragpick[rerank]"

On the bundled example dataset (keyword-heavy support questions), hybrid beats naive on hit rate and MRR even with the offline fake embedder:

ragpick eval examples/eval.jsonl --config examples/naive.yaml --config examples/hybrid.yaml

docs.title: parent_child
docs.text:
document ─→ parent sections (2000 chars) ─→ child chunks (400 chars) ─→ indexed
query ─→ hybrid search over children ─→ dedupe by parent ─→ parent sections ─→ generator

Small chunks are precise to search but often too small to answer from; large chunks give context but match poorly. parent_child does both: it searches children and hands the LLM each matching child's whole parent section. Each child stores its parent's text in metadata (parent_id, parent_text), so it works with every store and needs no extra document store. Citations and contexts use parent ids (manual.md#3).

blueprint: parent_child
components:
  chunker:
    params: {parent_size: 2000, parent_overlap: 0, child_size: 400, child_overlap: 50}
  retriever:
    params: {k: 5, base: hybrid, child_k: 20}   # base: hybrid | vector
query:
  top_k: 3        # parents are big: fewer contexts keep prompts reasonable

Trade-offs: bigger prompts, and parent text is stored once per child. Set requirements.long_documents: true and ragpick recommend will suggest it.

docs.title: corrective
docs.text:
query → base retrieval (hybrid) → grade each context ─┬─ enough relevant → generator
                                                      └─ too few → rewrite query → retrieve → grade
                                                                   └─ still none → "I don't know"

Plain RAG answers from whatever it retrieved, even when that's irrelevant, and that is where many hallucinations come from. corrective checks first:

  • Grading asks the LLM which passages actually help answer the question (one call per query). With the offline fake generator, a lexical test (share of question terms present) is used instead.
  • Correction. If fewer than min_relevant contexts pass, an LLM rewrites the query (exact terms kept, synonyms added) and it retrieves again. Offline, it searches deeper in the ranking instead.
  • Refusal. If nothing relevant is found, no contexts are passed on and the answer is "I don't know." (on_failure: keep falls back to the ungraded contexts.)
blueprint: corrective
components:
  retriever:
    params: {base: hybrid, grader: auto, min_relevant: 1, rewrite: true, on_failure: empty}
  generator: {type: openai, params: {model: gpt-4o-mini}}   # enables LLM grading

base: parent_child combines it with parent-child retrieval (set the chunker to parent_child too). Run ragpick query --trace to see the grade/rewrite steps. Set requirements.strict_grounding: true and the selector recommends it.

docs.title: graph
docs.text:
ingest:  chunk → extract entities & relations (LLM or heuristic) → knowledge graph
query:   question entities → expand N hops → graph-ranked chunks ─┐
         hybrid BM25 + vector ────────────────────────────────────┴→ RRF → [facts, chunks…]

Some questions need two facts that live in different places ("which error code relates to the battery of the thermostat that runs without a C-wire?"). graph links entities across chunks, so retrieval can follow those connections, and the LLM gets them spelled out:

Knowledge graph facts:
- LM-200 → related to → LM-300 Pro (source: getting-started.md#0)
- E-1042 → related to → AAA (source: error-codes.md#0)

blueprint: graph
components:
  retriever:
    params: {hops: 1, extractor: auto, graph_weight: 1.0, include_facts: true, max_facts: 15}
  generator: {type: openai, params: {model: gpt-4o-mini}}   # enables LLM extraction
  • Extraction. With a real LLM (extractor: auto or llm), each chunk is turned into typed entities and labelled relations ("requires", "is covered by") at ingest. That's one LLM call per chunk, so enable the cache. Offline, a heuristic picks up product codes, IDs, acronyms and multi-word names, and relates entities that share a sentence.
  • Access control. Chunks are filtered by allowed_groups as usual, and a fact is included only if at least one chunk visible to the caller supports it.
  • Evaluation. The facts context is marked synthetic and doesn't count in retrieval metrics.
  • Global search. After ingest, related entities are grouped into communities (label propagation), and each community gets a short summary: LLM-written, or a template offline. Unchanged communities keep their summaries, so re-ingesting doesn't re-pay for them. Questions like "what are the main themes?", "give an overview of …" or "summarise …" (mode: auto) are answered from the most relevant summaries instead of individual chunks. mode: global / local forces one or the other. A summary is shown only if the caller can see every chunk it was built from, so summaries never mix in restricted content.

Set requirements.multi_hop: true and the selector recommends it.

docs.title: agentic
docs.text:
question → search ─┐
           plan ───┼→ search (sub-question / follow-up) ─┐
           plan ───┴→ … up to max_steps ──────────────────┴→ RRF over all searches → generator

"How do I reset my password and how much does Lumen Plus cost?" needs two lookups. The agentic retriever searches for the question, then lets the LLM decide whether to run another search (and with what query) or finish, up to max_steps. It stops early when searches stop finding anything new. All result lists are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

blueprint: agentic
components:
  retriever:
    params: {base: hybrid, max_steps: 4, per_search_k: 4, planner: auto}
  generator: {type: openai, params: {model: gpt-4o-mini}}   # enables the LLM planner

Offline (or with planner: decompose), multi-part questions are split on "and", "vs", "compared to", ; and sentence breaks, and each part is searched. Every search goes through the base retriever (hybrid, vector, parent_child or graph) with the caller's filters, so access control holds. ragpick query --trace shows each agent_plan and agent_search step. Set requirements.complex_questions: true and the selector recommends it.

docs.title: sql
docs.text:
question + schema → LLM writes one SELECT → SQLite (read-only) → result rows → generator

For structured data, retrieval is the wrong tool: "how many LM-300s did we sell in October?" needs SUM, not similar text. The sql blueprint lets the LLM write the query and answers from the real result rows, citing the SQL.

blueprint: sql
data: tables                      # CSV files: one table per file (loader type: csv)
components:
  retriever:
    params:
      # database: ./shop.sqlite                     # …or an existing SQLite file
      # database: ${SHOP_DATABASE_URL}              # …or postgresql://reader:…@host/db
      table_groups: {salaries: [hr]}
      max_rows: 50
  generator: {type: openai, params: {model: gpt-4o-mini}}   # needs a real LLM

Safety is enforced by SQLite, not by the prompt:

Layer What it stops read-only connection (mode=ro, query_only) any write, even if everything else failed authorizer allow-list anything but SELECT/reads/functions (ATTACH, PRAGMA, writes in CTEs), reads of hidden tables and of sqlite_master statement check multiple statements, non-SELECT statements timeout and row cap runaway queries, huge results

PostgreSQL (database: postgresql://…, pip install "psycopg[binary]"): sessions are READ ONLY with a statement_timeout; administrative, file and network functions (pg_*, lo_*, dblink, set_config, …) are rejected; and before running a query, EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) lists every table the plan reads, so a hidden table is denied even through a view, CTE or subquery. Connect with a role that can only SELECT the tables you expose (that's the real boundary), use schemas: [...] to pick schemas, and list views over restricted tables in table_groups too, so they don't appear in the schema the LLM sees.

A failed query is retried once with the error message. Denied access is never retried, so a model can't probe for hidden tables.

Access control is table-level. table_groups: {salaries: [hr]} hides the table from the schema the LLM sees and denies it in the authorizer, unless the caller is in hr (--groups hr). There is no row-level security: split restricted rows into their own table. ragpick bench skips sql unless you pass -b sql.

docs.title: Adding a blueprint
docs.text:
A blueprint is one YAML file in src/ragpick/blueprints/:

metadata:
  name: my_blueprint
  description: One paragraph on what it does.
  best_for: [...]
  tradeoffs: [...]
  status: stable          # or planned
defaults:
  components: {...}       # same schema as rag.yaml `components`
  query: {top_k: 5}

Add a test that builds it (see tests/test_blueprints.py) and, if it should be recommended, a selector rule. See CONTRIBUTING.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A pipeline is made of small, swappable components. Each one is a typing.Protocol in ragpick.interfaces, so any object with the right methods works. No base class is needed.

Kind Protocol Built-in types loader load(path) -> Iterable[Document] directory, text, pdf, csv, langchain, llamaindex chunker split(docs) -> list[Chunk] recursive, fixed, parent_child, none embedder embed(texts), dimension (optional embed_query) fake, openai, sentence_transformers, langchain, llamaindex store add, search, delete, persist, load memory, qdrant keyword_index add, search, persist, load bm25 retriever retrieve(query, k, filters) vector, keyword, hybrid, parent_child, corrective, graph, agentic, sql, langchain, llamaindex reranker rerank(query, chunks, top_n) none, cross_encoder generator generate(query, contexts) -> Answer (optional stream) fake, openai, ollama, langchain, llamaindex

Data flows through these models: Document → Chunk → RetrievedChunk → Answer (text, citations as chunk ids, contexts, usage).

Ingest: loader → chunker → embedder → store (+ keyword index) → persisted to index_dir.

Query: retriever (with ACL filters) → reranker → generator → Answer.

Components receive embedder, store, keyword_index, generator and index_dir by constructor parameter name. A component that implements index_documents(docs) also receives the raw documents at ingest (the SQL retriever builds its database this way), and one that implements index_chunks(chunks) receives the chunks (the graph retriever builds its knowledge graph this way).

Streaming: pipeline.stream(question) yields StreamEvents: contexts, then delta text pieces, then the final answer with citations.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
A blueprint is a named, tested architecture: a YAML file with metadata (description, best_for, tradeoffs, status) and default components. Your rag.yaml names a blueprint and overrides only what differs:

blueprint: hybrid
components:
  embedder:  {type: openai, params: {model: text-embedding-3-small}}
  generator: {type: openai, params: {model: gpt-4o-mini}}

See Blueprints for the catalogue and roadmap.

docs.title: Architecture as code
docs.text:
rag.yaml is validated by Pydantic. Mistakes are reported with their YAML key path:

Invalid configuration in rag.yaml:
  - query.topk: unknown key (check for typos)
  - components.retriever: required key is missing (set it, or choose a `blueprint` that provides it)

Layers merge as blueprint defaults → rag.yaml → --set flags. Secrets come from the environment with ${OPENAI_API_KEY} and are never written back to disk. Check the merged result with ragpick validate.

docs.title: The selector
docs.text:
ragpick recommend runs a table of explainable rules over your requirements:

Situation Effect multi_hop (facts spread across documents) graph complex_questions (multi-part, comparisons) agentic multi_tenant reason: enable tenancy (see Multi-tenancy) long, structured documents parent_child small corpus, not keyword-heavy naive keyword-heavy, or medium/large corpus hybrid structured data (csv, sql, sqlite, …) sql (warns about row-level ACL; mixed data → use a router) strict_grounding (wrong answers are costly) corrective (over parent_child for long documents) latency: low reranker disabled, with a reason access_control with a store that cannot filter warning large corpus on the in-memory store warning, suggests Qdrant pdf data without ragpick[pdf] warning

To settle it with data instead of rules, ragpick bench runs every stable blueprint on your documents and questions; see Evaluation.

Every recommendation lists reasons, alternatives and warnings. The rules live in ragpick.selector.rules.RULES and are easy to extend.

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
Document-level access control is built in. Attach groups to a document with Markdown front matter (or any loader's metadata):

---
allowed_groups: [support]
---
# Internal escalation guide

Then query as a member of some groups:

p.query("How do I escalate?", groups=["support"])

ragpick query "How do I escalate?" --groups support

Rules:

  • Chunks without allowed_groups are public.
  • Chunks with it are returned only if the caller's groups intersect it.
  • groups=None (or no --groups) means public chunks only. This is secure by default.
  • Filtering happens inside every store and the BM25 index before ranking, so restricted text never reaches fusion, reranking, or the LLM.

Other metadata filters use the same mechanism: p.query(q, filters={"lang": ["en", "de"]}).

docs.title: Config reference
docs.text: Layers merge in this order: blueprint defaults → your rag.yaml → CLI --set. Within components, changing a component's type replaces it entirely; keeping the type merges params. Strings may use ${ENV_VAR} or ${ENV_VAR:-default}. Relative paths (data, index_dir) resolve against the config file's directory.

docs.title: Top level (rag.yaml)
docs.text:
Top-level schema of rag.yaml.

Key Type Default Description version 1 1 Config schema version. name str 'ragpick-app' Application name. blueprint str | null None Blueprint supplying default components. data str | null None Default source path for ragpick ingest / ragpick eval. requirements Requirements see section Inputs for ragpick recommend. components ComponentsConfig required Pipeline components (usually partly supplied by the blueprint). query QueryConfig see section Query-time settings. eval EvalConfig see section Evaluation settings. tracing TracingConfig see section Query tracing. cache CacheConfig see section Caching. serve ServeConfig see section HTTP API settings. tenancy TenancyConfig see section Multi-tenancy. index_dir str '.ragpick/index' Where indexes are persisted.

docs.title: requirements
docs.text:
What the application needs. Used by the selector (ragpick recommend).

Key Type Default Description data_types list[str] ['markdown'] Kinds of source data, e.g. markdown, pdf, html, sql, csv. corpus_size small | medium | large 'small' small (<1k chunks), medium, or large (>100k chunks). keyword_heavy bool False Queries rely on exact terms: product codes, legal terms, IDs. long_documents bool False Documents are long and structured (manuals, policies, contracts). complex_questions bool False Questions need several lookups (comparisons, multi-part questions). multi_tenant bool False Several customers' data must be kept in separate indexes. multi_hop bool False Questions connect facts spread across several documents. strict_grounding bool False Wrong answers are costly: prefer "I don't know" over guessing. latency low | normal 'normal' low disables expensive stages. needs_citations bool True Answers must cite their sources. access_control bool False Documents are restricted to groups (allowed_groups metadata).

docs.title: components
docs.text:
The components that make up a pipeline.

Key Type Default Description loader ComponentSpec required Turns a path into documents. chunker ComponentSpec required Splits documents into chunks. embedder ComponentSpec required Embeds chunks and queries. store ComponentSpec required Vector store. keyword_index ComponentSpec | null None Keyword index (required by the hybrid and keyword retrievers). retriever ComponentSpec required Retrieval strategy. reranker ComponentSpec see section Optional reranker. generator ComponentSpec required Answer generator (LLM).

docs.title: Component spec (each entry of components, and eval.judge)
docs.text:
A component reference: registry type plus constructor params.

Key Type Default Description type str required Registered component name, e.g. openai or bm25. params dict[str, Any] {} Keyword arguments passed to the component.

docs.title: query
docs.text:
Query-time settings.

Key Type Default Description top_k int 5 Number of contexts passed to the generator.

docs.title: eval
docs.text:
Evaluation settings.

Key Type Default Description judge ComponentSpec | null None Generator used as LLM judge (must support complete). prices dict[str, PriceSpec] {} Model name → price; merged over ragpick's built-in price table.

docs.title: Price spec (each entry of eval.prices)
docs.text:
Price of a model in USD per one million tokens.

Key Type Default Description prompt_per_1m float 0.0 completion_per_1m float 0.0

docs.title: tracing
docs.text:
Query tracing (nested, timed spans per stage).

Key Type Default Description enabled bool False Record a trace for every query. exporters list[ComponentSpec] [] Where traces go: jsonl (params: path) and/or console.

docs.title: cache
docs.text:
Persistent cache for embeddings and LLM calls.

Key Type Default Description enabled bool False Turn caching on. dir str '.ragpick/cache' Cache directory. embeddings bool True Cache embeddings. generations bool True Cache answers and LLM completions. ttl_seconds float | null None Expire entries after this age.

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
HTTP API settings for ragpick serve.

Key Type Default Description host str '127.0.0.1' Interface to bind. port int 8000 Port to bind. api_keys list[ApiKeySpec] [] If set, requests need Authorization: Bearer <key>. max_body_bytes int 65536 Largest accepted request body. cors_origins list[str] [] Origins allowed by CORS (* for any). allow_traces bool False Let clients request traces in responses.

docs.title: tenancy
docs.text:
Per-tenant indexes within one pipeline.

Key Type Default Description enabled bool False Each tenant gets an isolated index under <index_dir>/tenants/<id>. max_loaded int 32 Tenant indexes kept in memory (LRU).

docs.title: API key (each entry of serve.api_keys)
docs.text:
An API key for ragpick serve and the groups its holder may act as.

Key Type Default Description key str required The secret; use ${ENV_VAR} interpolation. name str 'client' Label used in logs. groups list[str] | null None Groups this key may query as (null = any groups the request names). tenant str | null None Bind the key to one tenant (null = the request picks the tenant).

docs.title: Router config (top level of a router file)
docs.text:
A config that routes each question to one of several pipelines.

Key Type Default Description version 1 1 Config schema version. name str 'ragpick-router' Application name. router RouterSpec required eval EvalConfig see section Evaluation settings. tracing TracingConfig see section Query tracing. serve ServeConfig see section HTTP API settings.

docs.title: router
docs.text:
How questions are routed.

Key Type Default Description strategy auto | llm | keywords 'auto' auto uses the LLM when one is available, else keywords. routes list[RouteSpec] required Possible destinations. default str | null None Fallback route (default: the first). fallback bool True Retry on the default route when the chosen one can't answer. llm ComponentSpec | null None Generator used to classify questions (default: a route's LLM).

docs.title: Route (each entry of router.routes)
docs.text:
One destination of a router: another pipeline config.

Key Type Default Description name str required Route name. config str required Path to the route's rag.yaml (relative to this file). description str '' What this route answers (shown to the LLM router). keywords list[str] [] Words/phrases that point to this route. groups list[str] | null None Only callers in these groups may be routed here.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Where the v0.1 brief left a choice open, ragpick picked the simplest option that keeps the interfaces extensible. Each decision is listed here so it can be revisited.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
1. Component type change replaces the component. When a layer (your YAML or a --set flag) changes a component's type, the blueprint's params for that component are dropped, because they belong to a different class (e.g. dimension for fake makes no sense for openai). If the type stays the same, params are merged key by key.
  2. CLI flags are generic --set key.path=value overrides, parsed as YAML scalars, instead of one flag per setting. A few common settings also have dedicated flags (query --top-k, query --groups).
  3. Relative paths resolve against the config file's directory, not the current directory, so ragpick eval --config examples/naive.yaml works from anywhere.
  4. New data key (optional) holds the default source path for ingest and is used by eval to build an index automatically when none exists.
  5. ${VAR} without a default fails loudly with the key path. ${VAR:-default} provides a fallback. Interpolation only happens in memory; ragpick init never writes secrets, and ragpick validate masks secret-looking keys (*key*, *token*, *secret*, *password*).
  6. components is required when no blueprint is set. There is no implicit default blueprint; the error message suggests setting one.

docs.title: Blueprints and components
docs.text:
1. Stable blueprints default to fake embedder and generator. A blueprint describes the architecture (chunking, retrieval, fusion, reranking); the model provider is a separate choice. This makes every blueprint runnable offline. ragpick init asks for a provider (fake, openai, ollama), and --yes defaults to fake. Using the fake generator is logged at INFO level.
  2. Planned blueprints are YAML files with metadata only. ragpick blueprints shows the roadmap from the same source of truth; loading one raises a clear error.
  3. Dependency injection by constructor parameter name. The pipeline passes embedder, store and keyword_index to any component whose constructor declares a parameter with that name. Plugins get the same treatment without registration hooks.
  4. A retriever that needs a keyword index gets bm25 automatically when components.keyword_index is not set.
  5. Re-ingest is an upsert per document: chunks of re-ingested documents are deleted first; other documents in the index are kept.
  6. Chunk ids are "<doc_id>#<n>"; doc ids are paths relative to the ingested directory. These ids are what relevant_doc_ids in eval datasets refer to.
  7. The index records its embedder in ragpick.json; querying with a different embedder config fails with a "re-ingest" message instead of returning garbage.
  8. Separate Registry instances start empty. Only the global registry loads built-ins, which keeps isolated tests simple. Registry.remove() exists for cleanup.
  9. Entry points are named "<kind>.<name>" and point at the factory. An entry point without a dot is just imported (side-effect registration). Broken plugins are logged and skipped.

docs.title: Access control and filters
docs.text:
1. Filters are a plain dict. A scalar value means equality, a list means in, list-valued metadata matches on intersection, and a chunk missing the key does not match.
  2. allowed_groups is special. Chunks without it are public, and chunks with it require a group intersection. allowed_groups: [] means "nobody".
  3. Secure by default. Pipeline.query(groups=None) returns public chunks only. ACL filtering happens inside the stores and BM25 before ranking, so restricted text never reaches fusion, reranking, or the LLM.
  4. Document metadata comes from Markdown front matter. That's how allowed_groups is attached to files. Programmatic loaders can set any metadata.
  5. Qdrant ACL: implemented as is_empty(allowed_groups) OR match_any(groups). Because Qdrant's is_empty also matches [], an empty list is stored as a private sentinel so "nobody" is not treated as "public".

docs.title: Generation
docs.text:
1. The model sees numeric citations [1]; Answer.citations holds chunk ids (stable, meaningful outside the prompt). Out-of-range numbers are ignored.
  2. No contexts → "I don't know." without calling the LLM.
  3. TextCompleter protocol (complete(system, user)) gives raw LLM access for judges; LLM generators implement both it and Generator. The fake generator's complete returns a fixed, configurable string (a constant-score fake judge for plumbing tests).
  4. Answer.usage.latency_ms covers the whole query (retrieval + generation).

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
1. Retrieval metrics are computed over the ranked context list mapped to doc_ids. precision@k divides by k even when fewer than k contexts are returned. Rows without relevant_doc_ids are excluded from retrieval averages.
  2. k is the config's query.top_k.
  3. Eval rows may carry groups, so access-controlled questions can be evaluated.
  4. eval --data PATH ingests into a temporary index per config, so comparisons never overwrite real indexes. Without --data, the config's existing index is used, built from data if missing.
  5. Cost is estimated for generation tokens only, from a built-in price table that eval.prices can extend or override. Unknown models show n/a. Judge tokens are not included.
  6. Judge failures and query errors are recorded per row and counted in errors; they don't abort the run.

docs.title: v0.2
docs.text:
1. Parent text lives in child metadata (parent_id, parent_text) instead of a new "document store" interface. It costs storage, but works unchanged with every VectorStore, BM25 and persistence path, including Qdrant.
  2. parent_child retriever wraps a base retriever (hybrid default, or vector) and fetches child_k (default 4 * k) children to find k distinct parents. Parent contexts get the best child's score and keep the child's source.
  3. Selector: long_documents (priority 60) beats keyword_heavy (50), because parent_child already uses hybrid search for children. Structured data (100) still wins.
  4. ragpick bench uses one top_k for every blueprint (base config's, or 5), otherwise metrics are not comparable. The base config supplies providers; architecture keys (chunker, keyword_index, retriever, reranker) always come from each blueprint. Ties on the metric go to lower p50 latency. The written winner config is built from the uninterpolated base YAML, so ${ENV_VAR} secrets are never expanded into it.
  5. Adapters depend on nothing. They call public methods (embed_documents, invoke, get_text_embedding_batch, …) and build objects from class_path + kwargs, so ragpick doesn't pin LangChain/LlamaIndex versions. The inner constructor arguments are called kwargs to avoid confusion with the component's own params.
  6. External retrievers are post-filtered for metadata filters and allowed_groups, because they can't apply ragpick filters themselves.
  7. embed_query is an optional embedder method, used by retrievers for queries when present (asymmetric models), so the Embedder protocol stays unchanged.
  8. setup-uv is pinned to an exact version (v10.3.3) because it no longer publishes major tags, and sets activate-environment: true, which newer versions no longer imply.

docs.title: v0.3
docs.text:
1. Tracing is built in and dependency-free: a context-variable span stack whose span()/set_attributes() are no-ops without an active trace. OpenTelemetry and similar backends are trace_exporter plugins rather than a dependency.
  2. Cache = one SQLite file, keyed by SHA-256 of (namespace, component fingerprint, input). Generator fingerprints include the system prompt, so prompt changes invalidate answers. Cached answers report usage.cached = True and zero tokens.
  3. The generator is built before the retriever and injected by name, so retrievers that need an LLM (corrective, sql) reuse the pipeline's (cached, traced) model.
  4. corrective grades in one LLM call per round (all passages in one prompt), not one call per passage. An unparseable grader reply keeps all contexts and logs a warning (fail open on parsing, so a flaky model doesn't silence every answer). grader: auto uses lexical grading for fake generators (is_fake = True).
  5. Corrective refusal returns zero contexts, and the generator answers "I don't know" without an LLM call. on_failure: keep opts out.
  6. SQL uses the standard-library sqlite3 with defence in depth: read-only URI + query_only, an authorizer that allows only SELECT/READ/FUNCTION/RECURSIVE and only reads of visible real tables, single-SELECT validation, a progress-handler timeout and a row cap. CTE names aren't tables; reads inside CTEs are checked individually. Other databases (Postgres, …) can come later behind the same retriever.
  7. SQL access control is table-level (table_groups), enforced in both the schema prompt and the authorizer; row-level security is out of scope. Access-denied errors are not retried, so the model can't probe.
  8. CSV ingest goes through a DocumentIndexer hook: the csv loader yields one document per file, the none chunker keeps the vector store empty, and the SQL retriever builds <index_dir>/sql/data.sqlite. With database: set, no ingest is required (requires_ingest = False).
  9. The sql blueprint defaults to the fake generator like every blueprint (so building it never needs a key), and the retriever explains at query time that SQL needs a real LLM. Blueprints declare data: documents | structured; bench compares document ones.

docs.title: v0.4
docs.text:
1. Routing composes whole pipelines (a router config lists route rag.yaml files) rather than adding a "router retriever", because SQL and document pipelines differ in ingest, index and data. Nested routers are rejected to keep traces and evaluation simple.
  2. Router LLM defaults to the first route's real LLM; auto silently uses keywords without one, while strategy: llm fails loudly. Invalid LLM replies fall back to keyword scoring, not an error.
  3. Fallback goes to the default route only (one retry), triggered by "I don't know", no contexts, or a failed SQL query. Route errors (e.g. configuration) are raised, not swallowed.
  4. Route groups gate routing itself, so a caller can never reach (or learn about by being routed to) a route outside their groups.
  5. The HTTP server has no dependencies: one framework-independent App.handle, exposed as an ASGI app (uvicorn if installed) and via ThreadingHTTPServer. Engine calls run in a worker thread under ASGI.
  6. API keys are bound to groups. Requests may narrow but never widen their key's groups; omitted groups mean the key's groups. Without keys, request groups are trusted, and serve warns on non-loopback hosts. /health stays unauthenticated for load balancers.
  7. Errors don't leak internals over HTTP: provider and configuration errors become 502/500 with a generic message; details go to the server log.
  8. The OpenTelemetry exporter replays finished traces rather than instrumenting live, so ragpick's tracing stays dependency-free and every backend sees identical spans. Root spans carry a wall-clock timestamp for absolute times.

docs.title: v0.5
docs.text:
1. Streams are events, not raw text: contexts first (so UIs can show sources while the answer is written), then deltas, then the full Answer with parsed citations. Generators without stream() produce one delta. Streams aren't traced (generators and context variables don't mix reliably), and routers don't fall back mid-stream.
  2. Streamed HTTP responses retrieve before streaming, so "not ingested" and validation errors keep proper status codes; later failures end the stream with an error event that hides provider details.
  3. GraphRAG v1 is local search: entity matching + N-hop expansion fused with hybrid search by RRF, plus a facts context. Global "themes" search needs community summarisation and is deferred.
  4. Graph extraction runs through a ChunkIndexer hook and is persisted as JSON next to the other indexes; the graph stores chunk copies (like BM25) so it can return chunks and check their metadata. Re-ingest replaces a document's graph contributions.
  5. The offline extractor is deliberately conservative: codes, acronyms and multi-word capitalised names only (single capitalised words are mostly UI labels and sentence starts), with codes kept inside longer names so "LM-300" links to "LM-300 Pro".
  6. Graph facts respect access control by requiring a supporting chunk the caller can see, so relations learned from restricted documents never appear for others.
  7. Synthetic contexts (metadata.synthetic) are excluded from retrieval metrics, since they aren't documents.
  8. PostgreSQL table checks use EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) relation lists, which see through views, CTEs and subqueries, plus read-only sessions, statement_timeout and a function denylist. A least-privilege database role remains the primary boundary. psycopg is loaded lazily with a custom install hint (no new extra).

docs.title: v0.6
docs.text:
1. Communities use deterministic weighted label propagation (stdlib, reproducible, near-linear) rather than Louvain/Leiden; it's good enough for summarising themes. Communities have at least two entities.
  2. Community summaries are keyed by a signature of members, relations and supporting chunks, and reused while unchanged, so re-ingest only re-summarises what changed.
  3. Global search returns community summaries as synthetic contexts (the generator does the "reduce" step); there is no separate map step per community, which keeps it to one LLM call. Questions route to global search by cue phrases (mode: auto), and fall back to local search if no visible summary matches.
  4. A summary is visible only if all its supporting chunks are visible (conservative: a summary can't be partially redacted, so any restricted source hides it).
  5. Agentic retrieval is a retriever, not a chat agent: it plans searches and returns fused contexts, so the grounded generator, citations, evaluation and access control stay unchanged. It always searches the original question first; repeats, two idle searches in a row, or max_steps end the loop. Unparseable plans count as "finish".
  6. Tenancy creates a child pipeline per tenant with its own index directory and fresh stateful components (store, keyword index, retriever), sharing stateless ones (embedder, generator, cache). An LRU bounds memory. Tenant ids are restricted to a filesystem-safe pattern before any path is built.
  7. Tenancy is explicit both ways: multi-tenant pipelines require a tenant, normal pipelines reject one (a TenantError, HTTP 400). Tenant-bound API keys override and restrict the request's tenant (403 on mismatch).

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
1. types-PyYAML is not a dev dependency (it wasn't in the approved list), so mypy treats yaml as untyped via an override. Adding the stub package would be a one-line improvement.
  2. Interactive questions use rich.prompt (Prompt.ask(choices=...), Confirm.ask). Recent typer releases no longer depend on click and typer.prompt does not accept choice types; rich is already a core dependency, so this works on every supported typer version.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Choosing a blueprint should be backed by numbers from your data. ragpick eval runs one or more configs over a question set and prints a comparison table.

docs.title: Dataset format
docs.text:
JSON Lines, one question per line. Only question is required:

{"question": "What does error E-1042 mean?", "ground_truth": "Low battery.", "relevant_doc_ids": ["error-codes.md"]}
{"question": "When do we escalate to Tier 2?", "relevant_doc_ids": ["internal-escalation.md"], "groups": ["support"]}
Field Purpose question The query. relevant_doc_ids Document ids (paths relative to the ingested directory) that answer it. Enables retrieval metrics. ground_truth Reference answer, stored in the results for review. groups Run the query as a member of these groups (to evaluate access-controlled content). id Optional identifier.

Blank lines and lines starting with # or // are ignored. Errors name the file and line.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
# compare two configs; each gets a temporary index built from --data
ragpick eval examples/eval.jsonl \
  --config examples/naive.yaml --config examples/hybrid.yaml \
  --data examples/data --output results.json

Without --data, each config uses its persisted index and builds it from the config's data path if none exists. --output writes .json (all rows) or .csv (one row per config).

From Python:

from ragpick import Pipeline
from ragpick.eval import evaluate, load_dataset

report = evaluate(Pipeline.from_yaml("rag.yaml"), load_dataset("eval.jsonl"))
print(report.metrics)

docs.title: Bench: try every blueprint
docs.text:
ragpick bench answers "which blueprint should I use?" with data. It runs every stable blueprint on your documents and questions, using the same models and the same top_k, and ranks them:

ragpick bench eval.jsonl --data ./docs --config rag.yaml --metric mrr --write best.yaml
  • Providers (loader, embedder, store, generator, eval settings) come from the base --config (default: ./rag.yaml if present, otherwise offline fake components).
  • Architecture (chunker, keyword index, retriever, reranker) comes from each blueprint.
  • --metric picks the winner: hit_rate@k, mrr (default), precision@k, or, with a judge, faithfulness / answer_relevance. Ties go to the lower median latency.
  • -b NAME (repeatable) limits the candidates; --top-k overrides k for all of them. By default only document blueprints are compared; sql answers from tables and needs a real LLM, so include it explicitly (-b sql) with a table dataset.
  • --write best.yaml saves the winner's config: your providers plus blueprint: <winner>. Secrets stay as ${ENV_VAR} references.
  • Each candidate gets a temporary index; your real indexes are never touched.
from ragpick.eval.bench import run_bench

result = run_bench("eval.jsonl", "./docs", base_config="rag.yaml", metric="mrr")
print(result.winner, result.ranking)

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Retrieval (no LLM needed). These are computed over the ranked contexts mapped to their doc_id, with k = query.top_k:

Metric Definition hit_rate@k 1 if any of the top-k contexts comes from a relevant document. mrr 1 / rank of the first relevant context (0 if none). precision@k relevant contexts in the top k, divided by k.

LLM-judged. These need a judge (eval.judge in the config or --judge openai:gpt-4o-mini):

Metric Question asked of the judge faithfulness Is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved contexts? answer_relevance Does the answer address the question directly?

Each score is 0–1 with a short reason per row (in the JSON output). All judge prompts live in ragpick/eval/prompts.py.

Operational:

Metric Definition latency_p50_ms / latency_p95_ms end-to-end query latency percentiles total_tokens prompt + completion tokens of the generator est_cost_usd from the price table (USD per 1M tokens); n/a for unknown models errors rows where the query or judge failed (recorded, not fatal)

Override or extend prices in the config:

eval:
  judge: {type: openai, params: {model: gpt-4o-mini}}
  prices:
    my-finetuned-model: {prompt_per_1m: 0.30, completion_per_1m: 1.20}

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• If cache is enabled, repeated runs reuse answers: costs drop to zero and latencies to near zero. Disable the cache when measuring latency.

  • 30–100 representative questions catch most regressions. Include the exact-term queries your users really send (codes, IDs), plus some that should return "I don't know".

  • Add eval to CI: run ragpick eval ... --output results.json and fail the build if hit_rate@k drops.
  • The fake generator and judge are for plumbing tests. Their answer metrics aren't meaningful, but retrieval metrics are.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
A trace records every stage of a query with its timing and key facts: what was retrieved, how many contexts passed grading, the SQL that ran, token counts, and whether the answer came from the cache.

ragpick query "What does error E-1042 mean?" --trace

query 2.4 ms  groups=0 blueprint=corrective
├── retrieve 0.7 ms  retriever=corrective k=5 attempts=1 kept=2 results=2
│   ├── vector_search 0.5 ms  k=5 results=5
│   ├── keyword_search 0.0 ms  k=5 results=2
│   └── grade 0.2 ms  grader=lexical contexts=5 relevant=2
├── rerank 0.0 ms  reranker=none top_n=3 results=2
└── generate 0.1 ms  generator=fake prompt_tokens=516 completion_tokens=33 cached=False

Record and export traces for every query:

tracing:
  enabled: true
  exporters:
    - {type: jsonl, params: {path: .ragpick/traces.jsonl}}   # one JSON object per query
    - {type: console}                                        # logs a tree (INFO level)

In Python, Pipeline.query(..., trace=True) sets answer.trace, a tree of Span objects (name, duration_ms, attributes, children, error). span.find("grade") looks up a stage.

Instrument your own components with the same helpers. They do nothing when tracing is off:

from ragpick.tracing import set_attributes, span


def retrieve(self, query, k, filters=None):
    with span("my_search", k=k):
        results = ...
        set_attributes(results=len(results))
        return results

OpenTelemetry. The otel exporter replays each trace as OpenTelemetry spans (ragpick.query, ragpick.retrieve, …) with the original timings, parent/child links, ragpick.* attributes and error status:

tracing:
  enabled: true
  exporters:
    - type: otel
      params:
        service_name: support-bot
        endpoint: http://localhost:4318/v1/traces   # optional, see below

Install OpenTelemetry yourself; it isn't a ragpick dependency. With only opentelemetry-api installed, spans go to whatever SDK your application already configures. With endpoint set (needs opentelemetry-sdk and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http), ragpick configures an OTLP/HTTP exporter itself. That's handy for ragpick serve and the CLI with Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, etc.

Other custom exporters (e.g. Langfuse) are plugins of kind trace_exporter: a class with export(root: Span), registered with @register("trace_exporter", "otel") or the ragpick.components entry point "trace_exporter.otel". A failing exporter is logged and never breaks a query.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Repeated work is expensive: re-ingesting unchanged documents re-embeds them, and re-running an evaluation pays for every answer again. Turn on the cache:

cache:
  enabled: true
  dir: .ragpick/cache        # a single SQLite file inside
  embeddings: true           # document and query embeddings
  generations: true          # answers and LLM completions (grading, SQL, rewrites)
  ttl_seconds: 604800        # optional: expire after 7 days
  • Keys are fingerprints. Each key hashes the component type, its params and the prompt version together with the input. Changing the model, temperature or prompt therefore never returns a stale result. Secrets in params only ever enter the cache inside a hash.
  • Cached answers are free: answer.usage.cached is True and token counts are 0, so evaluation cost estimates reflect what you actually paid.
  • Because cached answers return almost instantly, turn the cache off when you want ragpick eval / bench to measure real latency.
ragpick cache stats      # entries per kind
ragpick cache clear

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text: Any class that satisfies a protocol from ragpick.interfaces can be a component. Register it and refer to it by name in rag.yaml.

docs.title: 1. Implement the protocol
docs.text:
# ragpick_cohere/__init__.py
import cohere


class CohereEmbedder:
    """Cohere embeddings for ragpick."""

    def __init__(self, model: str = "embed-english-v3.0", api_key: str | None = None) -> None:
        self.model = model
        self._client = cohere.Client(api_key)

    @property
    def dimension(self) -> int:
        return 1024

    def embed(self, texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
        response = self._client.embed(texts=texts, model=self.model, input_type="search_document")
        return response.embeddings

Constructor keyword arguments become the component's params. ragpick validates them against the signature, so a typo in rag.yaml fails with the list of accepted params.

docs.title: In your own code (no packaging needed)
docs.text:
from ragpick import register


@register("embedder", "cohere")
class CohereEmbedder: ...

Import the module before building the pipeline.

docs.title: As an installable package (entry points)
docs.text:
# pyproject.toml of your plugin package
[project.entry-points."ragpick.components"]
"embedder.cohere" = "ragpick_cohere:CohereEmbedder"

The entry-point name is <kind>.<name>. Once the package is installed, type: cohere just works. An entry point whose name has no dot is simply imported, so a module can register several components with @register. Plugins can't shadow built-in names, and a broken plugin is logged and skipped.

docs.title: 3. Use it
docs.text:
blueprint: hybrid
components:
  embedder: {type: cohere, params: {model: embed-english-v3.0}}

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text:
Components that need other components declare them as constructor parameters named embedder, store or keyword_index. The pipeline passes them in:

@register("retriever", "mmr")
class MMRRetriever:
    def __init__(self, embedder, store, k: int = 10, diversity: float = 0.3) -> None: ...

    def retrieve(self, query, k, filters=None): ...

docs.title: Rules for stores and indexes
docs.text:
• Honour filters, including the allowed_groups access-control semantics. Reuse ragpick.filters.matches_filters, or translate filters natively as QdrantStore does.
  • Set supports_filters = True on the class so ragpick recommend doesn't warn users who need access control.
  • add must upsert by chunk id, and delete(doc_ids) must remove every chunk of those documents.

docs.title: Testing your plugin
docs.text:
Use the global registry and clean up afterwards, or build an isolated Registry():

from ragpick import Pipeline, registry


def test_my_embedder(tmp_path):
    registry.add("embedder", "mine", MyEmbedder)
    try:
        p = Pipeline.from_dict(
            {
                "blueprint": "naive",
                "index_dir": str(tmp_path),
                "components": {"embedder": {"type": "mine"}},
            }
        )
        p.ingest("tests/data")
        assert p.query("hello").contexts
    finally:
        registry.remove("embedder", "mine")

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Real assistants answer from more than one kind of source: manuals and an orders database, public FAQs and internal runbooks. A router sends each question to the pipeline best suited to answer it. Each route is an ordinary rag.yaml, so every blueprint, evaluation and access-control feature keeps working.

# router.yaml
version: 1
name: lumen-assistant
router:
  strategy: auto                # llm | keywords | auto
  default: docs                 # used when nothing matches, and for fallback
  fallback: true                # retry on `default` if the chosen route can't answer
  routes:
    - name: docs
      config: hybrid.yaml
      description: Product manuals, troubleshooting, error codes, warranty and policies
    - name: analytics
      config: sql.yaml
      description: Orders, sales, prices, quantities, counts and totals
      keywords: [how many, total, revenue, average, top, orders, sold]
      groups: [staff]           # only staff are ever routed here

Use it like any config:

ragpick validate -c router.yaml          # checks the router and every route config
ragpick ingest -c router.yaml            # ingests each route from its own `data`
ragpick query "How many LM-300 units did we sell?" -c router.yaml --groups staff --trace
ragpick eval eval.jsonl -c router.yaml   # per-question route is in the JSON output
ragpick serve -c router.yaml

from ragpick import load_engine

engine = load_engine("router.yaml")  # a Router (or a Pipeline for plain configs)
answer = engine.query("How many LM-300 units did we sell?", groups=["staff"])
print(answer.route, answer.text)

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
Strategy How it decides llm One LLM call with the route names and descriptions; the reply is {"route": "<name>"}. Uses router.llm if set, otherwise the first route with a real LLM generator. An invalid reply falls back to keywords. keywords Offline and deterministic: each keyword/phrase found in the question scores 2, each question word that appears in the description scores 1. The highest score wins; with no match, the default route is used. auto llm when an LLM is available, else keywords.

Good descriptions matter more than anything else: say what each source contains.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text: If the chosen route answers "I don't know", returns no contexts, or its SQL failed, and fallback is on, the question is re-asked on the default route. If that answers, its answer is returned (with answer.route set to the default). The trace shows a fallback span.

docs.title: Access control
docs.text:
• groups on a route restricts who can be routed there. Callers outside those groups are never sent to it, so the router can't leak a route's existence or data.
  • The caller's groups are passed through to the chosen pipeline, so document-level (allowed_groups) and SQL table-level (table_groups) rules still apply.

docs.title: Serving an HTTP API
docs.text:
ragpick serve exposes any config (a pipeline or a router) as a JSON API.

ragpick serve -c rag.yaml                         # http://127.0.0.1:8000
ragpick serve -c router.yaml --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

It runs on uvicorn when installed (pip install uvicorn, recommended for production) and falls back to Python's built-in threaded HTTP server otherwise. The application is a plain ASGI app, so you can also mount it in your own server:

from ragpick import load_engine
from ragpick.server import App, asgi_app

application = asgi_app(App(load_engine("rag.yaml")))  # uvicorn module:application

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method & path Body Returns GET /health – {"status": "ok" \| "not_ready", "version"}, 503 until ingested. No auth. GET /info – name, blueprint, version, routes (for routers) POST /query {"question", "groups"?, "filters"?, "top_k"?, "trace"?} {"text", "citations", "route", "contexts", "usage", "trace"?} POST /retrieve same {"contexts": [...]} (no generation) 
curl -s localhost:8000/query \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PORTAL_KEY" \
  -d '{"question": "How do I reset my password?"}'

Add "stream": true to get server-sent events instead of one JSON body: one contexts event, many delta events ({"text": "..."}), then a final answer event (the same JSON as a normal response). Retrieval errors still return a normal error status, because retrieval runs before the stream starts. A provider failure mid-stream ends the stream with an error event.

curl -N localhost:8000/query -d '{"question": "How do I reset my password?", "stream": true}'

Each context is {"id", "doc_id", "score", "source", "text", "metadata"}. Errors are {"error": "..."} with a meaningful status: 401/403 auth, 404, 405, 413 body too large, 422 invalid body, 502 model provider failed, 503 not ingested. Provider and configuration details are logged on the server, not returned to clients.

docs.title: Authentication and groups
docs.text:
serve:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8000
  api_keys:
    - {key: "${PORTAL_KEY}", name: support-portal, groups: [support]}
    - {key: "${HR_APP_KEY}", name: hr-app, groups: [hr, support]}
    - {key: "${ADMIN_KEY}", name: admin}          # groups: null → may act as any groups
  cors_origins: ["https://portal.example.com"]
  allow_traces: false
  max_body_bytes: 65536
  • With api_keys set, every endpoint except /health requires Authorization: Bearer <key> (compared in constant time).
  • The key decides the groups. A request that omits groups acts as all of its key's groups; a request may narrow them ("groups": [] is public-only) but can't add a group its key doesn't have (403). This is what makes document- and table-level access control safe over HTTP.
  • Without api_keys, request groups are trusted as sent. That's fine on localhost or behind your own authenticated backend; ragpick serve warns when binding a public interface without keys.
  • Keep keys in environment variables (${PORTAL_KEY}); they are never written to disk.

docs.title: Tenants
docs.text: With tenancy enabled, requests carry "tenant": "acme", or the API key fixes it (api_keys[].tenant); see Multi-tenancy.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Traces in responses are off unless serve.allow_traces: true. Server-side tracing (tracing.enabled, JSONL/OpenTelemetry exporters) works independently.
  • Turn on cache to make repeated questions instant and free.
  • One process loads the index into memory; for more throughput run several uvicorn workers behind a load balancer, with a shared vector database such as Qdrant.

docs.title: Multi-tenancy
docs.text:
SaaS products must keep each customer's documents apart. With tenancy enabled, one ragpick config (and one ragpick serve process) holds an isolated index per tenant:

blueprint: hybrid
tenancy:
  enabled: true
  max_loaded: 32          # tenant indexes kept in memory (least recently used are unloaded)
cache: {enabled: true}    # shared by all tenants

ragpick ingest ./customers/acme   --tenant acme
ragpick ingest ./customers/globex --tenant globex
ragpick query "What is our Gold plan price?" --tenant acme

pipeline = Pipeline.from_yaml("rag.yaml")
pipeline.ingest("./customers/acme", tenant="acme")
answer = pipeline.query("What is our Gold plan price?", tenant="acme", groups=["sales"])

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Each tenant's index lives in <index_dir>/tenants/<tenant>/, with its own vector store, BM25 index, knowledge graph and SQL database. Nothing is shared between tenants except the stateless parts: models and the embedding/answer cache.
  • Tenant pipelines are created on first use and kept in an LRU of max_loaded.
  • Tenant ids must be 1–64 letters, digits, - or _ (starting with a letter or digit). Anything else (../x, a/b) is rejected before touching the filesystem.
  • A multi-tenant pipeline refuses calls without a tenant, and a normal pipeline refuses calls with one, so a misconfiguration can't quietly fall back to the wrong index.
  • Document-level (allowed_groups) access control still applies inside each tenant.

docs.title: Over HTTP
docs.text:
Bind API keys to tenants so a client can only ever reach its own data:

serve:
  api_keys:
    - {key: "${ACME_KEY}", name: acme-portal, tenant: acme, groups: [support]}
    - {key: "${GLOBEX_KEY}", name: globex-portal, tenant: globex}
    - {key: "${ADMIN_KEY}", name: admin}        # no tenant: requests choose one

curl -s localhost:8000/query -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACME_KEY" \
  -d '{"question": "What is our Gold plan price?"}'

A tenant-bound key that sends a different "tenant" gets 403. Keys without a tenant must send "tenant" in the body (400 otherwise). Without API keys, the request's tenant is trusted, which is only appropriate behind your own authenticated backend.

Routers pass tenant through to their routes (the route configs must enable tenancy); ingest each route config per tenant.
